pumac-2020-geometry-b-01.title: Compare the two paths
pumac-2020-geometry-b-01.body:
Let the inner sidewalk have radius $r$ and the road have width $w$, so the outer sidewalk has radius $r+w$. For a turn of angle $\theta$:

- staying on the outside costs $(r+w)\theta$;
- crossing, walking the inner arc, and crossing back costs $w+r\theta+w=2w+r\theta$.

Crossing is worthwhile as soon as $2w+r\theta\le(r+w)\theta$, i.e. $2w\le w\theta$, i.e. $\theta\ge2$ (independent of $r$ and $w$). So $\theta=2$ and $\lfloor100\theta\rfloor=200$.

**Answer: 200**

pumac-2020-geometry-b-02.title: Hexagon plus centre, and a matching lower bound
pumac-2020-geometry-b-02.body:
**Construction.** Put one student at the centre of a circle of radius $6$ and six at the vertices of a regular hexagon inscribed in it. Adjacent vertices are $6$ apart, and each vertex is $6$ from the centre, so all distances are at least $6$. The diameter is $12$.

**No smaller circle works.** Suppose all seven points lie in a closed disc of radius $R<6$ with centre $O$. No point is at $O$, since then every other point would be within $R<6$ of it. So each point has a polar angle about $O$. Seven angles on a circle: two of them differ by at most $360^\circ/7<60^\circ$. For two points at distances $r_1\le r_2\le R$ from $O$ whose directions differ by $\varphi\le60^\circ$, the law of cosines gives
$$d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2-2r_1r_2\cos\varphi\le r_1^2+r_2^2-r_1r_2\le r_2^2 ,$$
so $d\le r_2\le R<6$, contradicting the $6$-foot rule. Hence $R\ge6$, the diameter is at least $12$.

**Answer: 12**

pumac-2020-geometry-b-03.title: Right trapezoid
pumac-2020-geometry-b-03.body:
Let $r=OQ=1$ and $s=PQ$. The radii $OD$ and $PE$ are both perpendicular to the common tangent $DE$, so $ODEP$ is a right trapezoid with parallel sides $OD=r$, $PE=s$ and height $DE$. For two externally tangent circles, the length of the common external tangent is
$$DE=\sqrt{(r+s)^2-(s-r)^2}=2\sqrt{rs}$$
(drop the perpendicular from $O$ to $PE$: hypotenuse $OP=r+s$, one leg $s-r$).

Therefore
$$[ODEP]=\frac{r+s}{2}\cdot2\sqrt{rs}=(r+s)\sqrt{rs}.$$
With $r=1$: $(1+s)\sqrt s=520$. The left side is increasing in $s$, and $s=64$ gives $65\cdot8=520$. So $PQ=64$.

**Answer: 64**

pumac-2020-geometry-b-04.title: Triangle $OAB$ with the incentre
pumac-2020-geometry-b-04.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of $\Omega$ and $r$ its radius. The centre of a circle tangent to the sides of an angle lies on its bisector, so $\angle OAB=\frac12\angle FAB=60^\circ$ and $\angle OBA=\frac12\angle ABC=75^\circ$. Let $\Omega$ touch $AB$ at $X$; then $OX=r$ is the altitude of triangle $OAB$, and
$$AX=r\cot60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}r,\qquad BX=r\cot75^\circ=(2-\sqrt3)r.$$
From $AX+BX=12$:
$$r\left(\frac{\sqrt3}3+2-\sqrt3\right)=r\cdot\frac{6-2\sqrt3}{3}=12\ \Rightarrow\ r=\frac{18}{3-\sqrt3}=\frac{18(3+\sqrt3)}{6}=9+3\sqrt3=9+\sqrt{27}.$$
So $m=9$, $n=27$ and $m+n=36$.

**Answer: 36**

pumac-2020-geometry-b-06.title: The locus is an ellipse
pumac-2020-geometry-b-06.body:
Let $C$ have radius $r$ and let $OP=x<r$. Take a circle with centre $X$ through $P$ and tangent (internally) to $C$. The point of tangency lies on line $OX$ and is at distance $XP$ from $X$ (it is on the circle), so the radius $r$ of $C$ equals $OX+XP$. Thus $OX+XP=r$ is constant, and $\Gamma$ is the ellipse with foci $O$ and $P$ and major axis $r$.

The semi-major axis is $\frac r2$ and the half-distance between the foci is $\frac x2$, so the semi-minor axis is $\sqrt{\frac{r^2}4-\frac{x^2}4}=\frac12\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$. Since $PQ\perp OP$, $PQ^2=r^2-x^2$, so
$$[\Gamma]=\pi\cdot\frac r2\cdot\frac12\sqrt{r^2-x^2}=\frac{\pi}{4}\,r\cdot PQ .$$

**Using the area condition.** $[C]=100[\Gamma]$ gives $\pi r^2=25\pi\,r\cdot PQ$, so $r=25\,PQ$.

The circle $D$ has diameter $PQ$, so $[D]=\frac\pi4PQ^2$ and
$$\frac{[C]}{[D]}=\frac{\pi r^2}{\frac\pi4PQ^2}=4\left(\frac{r}{PQ}\right)^2=4\cdot625=2500.$$

**Answer: 2500**

pumac-2020-geometry-b-07.title: Mass points, power of a point, Stewart
pumac-2020-geometry-b-07.body:
**Locate $E$ and $F$.** $BD=6$, $DC=16$. Give $B$ mass $8$ and $C$ mass $3$ so that $D$ balances them (mass $11$). Since $\frac{AK}{KD}=\frac{11}{7}$, $A$ must have mass $7$. Then
$$\frac{AF}{FB}=\frac{m_B}{m_A}=\frac87,\qquad\frac{AE}{EC}=\frac{m_C}{m_A}=\frac37,$$
so $AF=15\cdot\frac8{15}=8$ and $AE=20\cdot\frac3{10}=6$.

**$A$ lies on line $KL$.** The power of $A$ with respect to circle $BFK$ is $AF\cdot AB=8\cdot15=120$, and with respect to circle $CEK$ it is $AE\cdot AC=6\cdot20=120$. So $A$ has equal power with respect to both circles, hence lies on their radical axis $KL$, and $AK\cdot AL=120$.

**Length $AK$.** By Stewart's theorem on cevian $AD$ ($BD=6$, $DC=16$):
$$AB^2\cdot DC+AC^2\cdot BD=BC\,(AD^2+BD\cdot DC)\Rightarrow 225\cdot16+400\cdot6=22\,(AD^2+96),$$
so $22AD^2=6000-2112=3888$ and $AD^2=\frac{1944}{11}$. With $AK=\frac{11}{18}AD$: $AK^2=\frac{121}{324}\cdot\frac{1944}{11}=66$, so $AK=\sqrt{66}$.

**Finish.** $AL=\frac{120}{\sqrt{66}}$ and $K$ lies between $A$ and $L$, so
$$KL=AL-AK=\frac{120-66}{\sqrt{66}}=\frac{54}{\sqrt{66}},\qquad KL^2=\frac{2916}{66}=\frac{486}{11}.$$
Thus $a+b=486+11=497$.

**Answer: 497**

pumac-2020-geometry-b-08.title: Affine invariance
pumac-2020-geometry-b-08.body:
Every ellipse is the image of the unit circle under an affine map, and affine maps multiply all areas by the same constant. So for an ellipse through $A,B,C$,
$$\frac{[\text{ellipse}]}{[ABC]}=\frac{\pi}{[\text{triangle inscribed in the unit circle}]}.$$
Among triangles inscribed in a circle of radius $1$ the equilateral one has the largest area, $\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}$. Hence $\frac{[\text{ellipse}]}{[ABC]}\ge\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt3}=\frac{4\sqrt3\pi}{9}$, with equality attained (choose the affine map sending the unit circle's equilateral triangle to $ABC$).

By Heron, $[ABC]=84$. So the smallest area is
$$84\cdot\frac{4\sqrt3\pi}{9}=\frac{112\sqrt3\,\pi}{3}.$$
Thus $a=112$, $b=3$, $c=3$ and $a+b+c=118$.

**Answer: 118**
